analysis.one_liner: Charges the largest fossil fuel companies $1 trillion for past emissions to fund climate disaster response.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since January 7, 2025, with no hearing, markup, or vote ever scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge companies responsible for more than a billion metric tons of carbon dioxide released from their fossil fuel extraction and refining since 2000 a one-time assessment totaling $1 trillion, shared in proportion to each company's emissions. The money would go into a dedicated fund for climate disaster recovery, resilient infrastructure, and help for communities hit hardest, with 40 percent set aside for environmental justice communities. Companies could pay over nine years, and the bill explicitly leaves state lawsuits against polluters untouched.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities hit by climate-driven disasters such as hurricanes, floods, extreme heat, and wildfires, since the fund would pay for FEMA response and resilience programs, resilient infrastructure, and disaster planning. Communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal communities that face the worst pollution and disaster exposure would get 40 percent of the money. Federal, state, and local taxpayers also benefit, because climate disaster costs now running at least $150 billion a year are paid from general revenue rather than by the industry that produced the emissions.

how_it_helps.text: Companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from extraction or refining between 2000 and 2023 would pay a share of a $1 trillion assessment, proportional to their emissions, due September 30, 2026, with an optional nine-year installment plan [S2].

The money goes into a Polluters Pay Climate Fund used for disaster recovery, climate-resilient infrastructure, grid and food-system resilience, wildfire management, and public health, including at least $15 billion a year for FEMA programs and $6 billion a year for Clean Air Act climate grants [S2].

Forty percent of each year's fund spending must benefit environmental justice communities — communities of color, low-income communities, and Tribal and Indigenous communities that bear the worst pollution and disaster impacts [S2].

The bill cites the Fifth National Climate Assessment finding that extreme weather already costs the United States at least $150 billion a year, disproportionately hitting underserved communities [S2].

The bill expressly does not preempt state and local climate laws or lawsuits for deception, nuisance, negligence, or failure to warn over climate damage, so states and citizens keep their own remedies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The largest fossil fuel producers and refiners — those whose operations and products released more than a billion metric tons of carbon dioxide between 2000 and 2023, roughly the biggest oil, gas, and coal companies — would pay up to $1 trillion in aggregate, and the tax could not be deducted as a business expense. To the extent companies raise fuel prices or cut investment to cover the charge, some cost would be passed on to consumers and shareholders.
analysis.who_pays_short: The biggest oil, gas, and coal companies

drawbacks.text: The assessment is retroactive, reaching emissions from 2000 through 2023 that were lawful at the time; a good-faith objection is that a company can fairly be charged only for future emissions, not for past activity [S2].

Because the charge falls on fuel production, companies would be expected to contest it in court and to pass part of the cost to consumers through higher fuel prices, which hit lower-income households hardest [S2].
The bill charges for past emissions but does not itself reduce future emissions or cap fossil fuel production, so it is a funding mechanism rather than a climate-impact prevention measure [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and targeted: a trillion dollars of disaster recovery and resilience funding would offset costs that taxpayers currently bear, and the money is steered toward the communities hurt most. The main honest costs are that the charge is retroactive and that companies will fight it and may pass some of it to consumers at the pump. Weighing that against $150 billion a year in publicly paid disaster costs, the bill's design directs the cost to the industry whose product created the emissions, which is the point of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on January 7, 2025, was read twice, and was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled for the rest of 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the bill with Senators Sanders, Merkley, Markey, and Warren as original cosponsors [S2].
On January 7, 2025, the bill was read twice in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Finance; the action history shows no further action since [S4].

The bill would impose a $1 trillion assessment on companies responsible for more than 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from fossil fuel extraction and refining between 2000 and 2023, allocated in proportion to each company's share of those emissions [S2].

Revenue would go to a dedicated fund for climate disaster response, resilience, and adaptation, with at least $15 billion a year to FEMA, $6 billion a year to Clean Air Act climate grants, and a 40 percent set-aside for environmental justice communities [S2].
Companies could elect to pay in nine annual installments beginning September 30, 2026, and the tax would not be deductible as a business expense [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the largest fossil fuel companies are better off: no assessment has been enacted and no committee action has moved the bill, so the $1 trillion liability exists only on paper. Communities facing climate disasters continue to rely on ordinary federal disaster funding rather than an industry-paid fund.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest fossil fuel companies, so far

for.name: Sen. Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Polluters Pay Climate Fund Act on January 7, 2025.

for.name: Sens. Sanders, Merkley, Markey, and Warren
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction; the bill's six total cosponsors are all Democrats or independents.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral on January 7, 2025 — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled through the rest of 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All seven supporters — the sponsor and six cosponsors — are Democrats or independents, and no Republican cosponsored; the Finance Committee, chaired by a Republican, took no action.

industries.industry: Large fossil fuel extractors and refiners (major oil, gas, and coal companies)
industries.note: Companies responsible for more than a billion metric tons of carbon dioxide from 2000 through 2023 would owe a proportional share of a $1 trillion assessment, not deductible as a business expense. Their interest in the bill runs against the public's because the money recovers disaster and adaptation costs that the public otherwise pays for fuel they sell.

industries.industry: State and local taxpayers and federal disaster programs (FEMA)
industries.note: The fund would route at least $15 billion a year into FEMA response and resilience programs, replacing general-revenue spending on climate disasters that already cost at least $150 billion a year.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Finance Committee chair, and no Republican cosponsor, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or markup this Congress. A bill in this position typically dies at the end of the two-year session unless reintroduced; the January 2026 payment date the bill sets is already unworkable, which further reduces prospects.
